query: Which sample sizes, power calculations, and statistical methods are suitable for nationwide surveys and pilot REC evaluations, and what are clear success criteria and decision rules?

response.query: Which sample sizes, power calculations, and statistical methods are suitable for nationwide surveys and pilot REC evaluations, and what are clear success criteria and decision rules?
response.answer: For nationwide surveys, use G*Power for power analysis; pilot studies typically sample 10% of the full study size. Success criteria include reliability and validity assessments, with a minimum of 70 subjects for external pilot studies.

results.content: Besides the significance level (*i.e*., alpha) and power (*i.e*., 1 – beta), there are 3 other parameters for the sample size calculation such as R0 refers to a pre-specified value of the intra-class coefficient in the null hypothesis, R1 refers to a pre-specified value of the intra-class coefficient in the alternative hypothesis and the number of total observations which are designated as 2 shall refer to the observations for performing the test-retest reliability. When assessing the validity and/or reliability of a questionnaire via a pilot study, a researcher will usually evaluate the test-retest reliability by performing the kappa agreement test or intra-class correlation test. Therefore, the researcher can only assess the reliability of a questionnaire in a pilot study whereas the validity of a questionnaire will have to be assessed by the actual full-scale surveys because the validation process will necessitate a much larger sample size [29,30]. Hence, this paper provides a list of useful recommendations regarding the determination of minimum sample size requirement when designing a pilot study to assess the reliability of the questionnaire.

results.title: How to figure out an appropriate sample for the pilot study?
results.content: According to Connelly (2008), extant literature suggests that a pilot study sample should be 10% of the sample projected for the larger parent study.
